Title: AKU celebrates World Children's Day
NewsSummary: "Playing too many video games and spending hours in front of the computer is leading to our children performing poorly at school, developing sleep disorders and becoming inactive and obese," said Dr Arshalooz Rehman,
NewsContent:
"Playing too many video games and spending hours in front of the computer is leading to our children performing poorly at school, developing sleep disorders and becoming inactive and obese," said Dr Arshalooz Rehman, Assistant Professor and Consultant Paediatrician, Aga Khan University (AKU), during an awareness programme held at the University on the occasion of World Children's Day, to discuss important health issues affecting children in Pakistan.

"While there are positive aspects of using computers and technology, children must be also go out and play so they can be active and exercise. Parents should monitor what children are watching and playing, and how much time they spend on the computer so that there is a balance between active and inactive play," said Dr Rehman.

Dengue fever and it affect on children was also discussed at the event. Dr Rizwan Haider, Senior Instructor and Consultant Paediatrician, AKU, said, "Since 1994, when the first confirmed epidemic of dengue fever in Pakistan occurred, there have been sporadic cases in different parts of the country and since 2005, regular epidemics have occurred each year in Pakistan, especially during the winter months." Dr Haider also noted that dengue fever is a viral illness that does not spread through coughing, but is transmitted through the bite of certain female mosquitoes. While in most cases, dengue causes mild fever, in severe cases, it may cause death due to bleeding and shock. Dengue-carrying mosquitoes breed in fresh water, are found indoors, and usually bite during the daytime. "Since there is no treatment or vaccine for dengue, it is best to try to reduce your exposure to mosquitoes. Use mosquito netting around the house, spray insecticides, and make sure that children use mosquito repellent lotions and creams. Also, ensure that water in containers is covered," said Dr Haider.

Dr Haider also discussed thalassemia, a hereditary blood disorder among children that causes anaemia in mild cases, and death in severe cases. "If both parents carry the defective thalassemia gene, a child has a 25 per cent risk of being born with thalassemia major, the severe form of the disease," said Dr Haider. About 6 per cent of the Pakistani population carries the milder, thalassemia minor gene, which usually requires no treatment. Blood screening of adults is the only way to diagnose the disease and should be done at three stages: first, before a couple gets married, then before a child is conceived, and finally, the screening of a child after birth. "These strategies have successfully eradicated thalassemia in many countries across the world, and can easily be adopted in Pakistan also," said Dr Haider.

Stressing the harms of anaemia and iron deficiency in children, Dr Ahmed Naqvi, Associate Professor and Paediatric Haematologist and Oncologist, AKU, said that children in poor countries are more likely to suffer from anaemia and iron deficiency, since many parents are unable to afford nutritious food for their family. Iron is needed for the formation of blood and other vital enzymes and compounds in the body. He added that the natural amount of iron at birth is only enough for the first six months of a baby's life, and milk is a poor source of iron that cannot meet the requirements of a rapidly growing body. He stressed that it is essential to add iron-rich food into a child's diet, including meat, fish, poultry, cereals and lentils. "Children with iron deficiency have decreased attentiveness, cognitive performance and mental and motor development. Anaemia can be corrected within six to eight weeks with iron supplements, but the effect on a child's mental and motor development may be long lasting," said Dr Naqvi.

Dr Naqvi added that the lack of other nutrients, like vitamin B12 and folic acid may cause severe malnutrition; therefore vegetarian diets should be avoided. Since vitamin C enhances iron absorption, fruits such as citrus, tomatoes and potatoes should be added to the diet. Tea slows down iron absorption and should not be taken with meals.
